level.betsy_ross.title: A Star in One Snip
level.betsy_ross.goal: A Philadelphia seamstress shows General Washington how to cut a star with a single snip of the scissors, then sews the first flag
level.betsy_ross.hint: A sketch isn't an order: six-pointed stars take ages to sew. Show your customers an easier way.
level.betsy_ross.intro: Philadelphia, 1776. According to family tradition, three men walk into the shop of the widowed upholsterer Betsy Ross: General George Washington, financier Robert Morris, and her late husband's uncle George Ross. They carry a sketch of a flag for the new nation: thirteen stripes and thirteen six-pointed stars.
level.betsy_ross.fact: According to family tradition, Betsy told the general the star should have five points, folded a scrap of cloth, and with one snip of her scissors cut a perfect star. The committee was amazed, and she sewed a flag with thirteen stars in a circle. On June 14, 1777, Congress adopted a flag of 13 stripes and 13 stars without specifying how they should be arranged, and the day is still celebrated as Flag Day. Betsy's story was first made public by her grandson in 1870 and no documents back it up, but the Betsy Ross House in Philadelphia is one of the city's most visited museums.
level.betsy_ross.source: William Canby, paper read to the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (1870); Flag Resolution of the Continental Congress (1777)
level.rip_van_winkle.title: Rip Van Winkle
level.rip_van_winkle.goal: A good-natured idler falls asleep in the mountains a subject of the British king and wakes up a citizen of a republic
level.rip_van_winkle.hint: First he has to leave home; otherwise he'll never reach the mountains. Once he wakes, ask what has changed before drinking to anyone.
level.rip_van_winkle.intro: A village at the foot of the Catskills in the Hudson Valley, long before the Revolution. Rip Van Winkle is everyone's favorite, ready to help any neighbor except his own wife. One day, fleeing her scolding, he heads into the mountains with his gun and his dog.
level.rip_van_winkle.fact: In the mountains Rip meets strange, silent men in old-fashioned Dutch clothes, the ghosts of Hendrick Hudson's crew, playing ninepins, and he samples their liquor. He falls asleep and wakes with a gray beard down to his waist. The village has become a stranger: the inn sign shows General Washington instead of King George, and people are shouting about elections and the rights of citizens. Out of habit Rip declares himself a loyal subject of the king and is nearly taken for a spy. He has slept twenty years, straight through the Revolution. His scolding wife has died in the meantime, the one change he does not regret. Washington Irving's 1819 tale became one of the first American literary myths.
level.sleepy_hollow.title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow
level.sleepy_hollow.goal: A country schoolmaster courts a rich heiress, hears one too many tales of the Headless Horseman, and vanishes forever
level.sleepy_hollow.hint: The strongman doesn't need a fight: fear will do the work for him. But you can only frighten someone who stays at the party late.
level.sleepy_hollow.intro: Sleepy Hollow, a Dutch hamlet on the Hudson. The lanky, superstitious schoolmaster Ichabod Crane dreams of marrying Katrina Van Tassel, and her father's farms along with her. Katrina has another suitor: the burly prankster Brom Bones.
level.sleepy_hollow.fact: One autumn evening at the Van Tassels' party, the guests told ghost stories, among them the tale of a Hessian trooper whose head was carried off by a cannonball and who rides by night in search of it. Heading home after midnight, Ichabod heard hoofbeats behind him: a headless horseman was on his trail. At the church bridge the rider hurled his head at the schoolmaster, and Ichabod was never seen again. In the morning they found his horse, his hat, and a shattered pumpkin. Brom Bones soon married Katrina, and whenever that night came up, he wore a knowing smile. Washington Irving's 1820 story became the first American Gothic legend, and the pumpkin on the road became its symbol.
level.sleepy_hollow.source: Washington Irving, "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow" (1820)
level.johnny_appleseed.title: Johnny Appleseed
level.johnny_appleseed.goal: A barefoot wanderer with a pot on his head plants apple nurseries along the settlers' road west
level.johnny_appleseed.hint: Seeds come from where apples get pressed. Grafting sweet varieties is someone else's method: our orchardist thought it hurt the tree.
level.johnny_appleseed.intro: The early 1800s. Settlers are pushing west through Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Indiana. Ahead of them walks John Chapman, barefoot, dressed in sackcloth and, so the stories go, wearing a cooking pot for a hat. People call him Johnny Appleseed.
level.johnny_appleseed.fact: Chapman gathered seeds at Pennsylvania cider mills and planted nurseries where settlers were bound to arrive a few years later, then sold them the seedlings. It paid: under the rules of Ohio land companies, a settler had to plant 50 apple trees to secure a claim. Chapman refused to graft his trees, believing that cutting them was cruel, so his seeds grew sour wild apples. Few were eaten; they went into cider and applejack. He was a Swedenborgian preacher and a vegetarian, and he died in 1845 owning a good deal of land. His last surviving tree, legend has it, still grows in Ohio.
level.johnny_appleseed.source: Michael Pollan, "The Botany of Desire" (2001); W. D. Haley, "Johnny Appleseed: A Pioneer Hero" (1871)
level.john_henry.title: John Henry
level.john_henry.goal: A Black steel-driving man races a steam drill in a tunnel, wins, and dies with his hammer in his hand
level.john_henry.hint: No bet, no contest, and a machine bought without one just replaces the men. After the hero falls, the hammer doesn't hit the ground.
level.john_henry.intro: The mountains of West Virginia, the 1870s. The railroad is boring a tunnel through Big Bend Mountain. Steel drivers, many of them only recently freed from slavery, pound steel drills into the rock by hand. The strongest of them all is John Henry. One day a steam drill arrives in camp.
level.john_henry.fact: As the ballad tells it, John Henry said to the captain, "A man ain't nothing but a man, but before I let your steam drill beat me down, I'll die with a hammer in my hand." Swinging a hammer in each hand, he drove more steel in a day than the machine, then dropped dead. His wife, Polly Ann, picked up the hammer and "drove steel like a man." Whether John Henry really lived is still debated: historian Scott Nelson found a prisoner named John William Henry whom the Virginia penitentiary leased out to build railroad tunnels. The ballad became a workers' anthem and one of the most recorded songs in America.
level.john_henry.source: Scott Reynolds Nelson, "Steel Drivin' Man: John Henry, the Untold Story of an American Legend" (2006); the ballad "John Henry" (19th century)
level.paul_bunyan.title: Paul Bunyan and the Blue Ox
level.paul_bunyan.goal: A giant lumberjack finds a calf in the blue snow, feeds the camp on pancakes, and straightens a river
level.paul_bunyan.hint: No ox, no straight river, and a hungry giant can't pull a thing. The books can wait.
level.paul_bunyan.intro: The North Woods of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota, the late 1800s. On long evenings in the logging camps, men swap tall tales, and their favorite hero is Paul Bunyan, a lumberjack so big that a single stride carries him seven miles.
level.paul_bunyan.fact: In the Winter of the Blue Snow, when even the snow fell blue, Paul found a frozen calf, warmed it up, and it stayed blue forever. That was Babe the Blue Ox, who measured 42 ax handles between the horns. Sourdough Sam the cook made the camp's pancakes on a griddle an acre wide, greased by kitchen boys skating across it with hams strapped to their feet. Babe hauled a crooked river by one end until it ran straight, and the footprints of Paul and Babe, they say, became Minnesota's ten thousand lakes. These tall tales were the oral folklore of lumberjacks; in the 1910s the Red River Lumber Company picked them up for its advertising, and Paul became a national hero. Giant statues of him stand in dozens of towns across North America.
level.paul_bunyan.source: James MacGillivray, "The Round River Drive" (Detroit News-Tribune, 1910); W. B. Laughead, Red River Lumber Company promotional booklets (1914)
level.cahokia.title: City of Mounds
level.cahokia.goal: Five centuries before the Europeans, a city larger than the London of its day rises on the Mississippi, with mounds, a solar calendar, and trade across half a continent
level.cahokia.hint: The city lives by the sun: calendar first, then building. A palisade is a tempting defense, but the forest isn't endless.
level.cahokia.intro: Around 1050, on the bank of the Mississippi across from present-day St. Louis. Here grows Cahokia, the largest city north of Mexico. We don't know the names of its people: they had no writing, and everything we know comes from archaeology. We'll call them by their roles.
level.cahokia.fact: At its height, around 1100, Cahokia was home to 10,000 to 20,000 people, more than London at the time. Its great mound, Monks Mound, was built by hand, basket by basket of earth: it rises more than 100 feet, and its base covers more ground than the Great Pyramid of Giza. A circle of wooden posts, nicknamed "Woodhenge," marked the solstices and equinoxes. Shells came here from the Gulf of Mexico, copper from the Great Lakes, and mica from the Appalachians. Around 1350 the city emptied out; scholars still debate why: droughts, floods, deforestation, war. Cahokia is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Our story of the United States begins not with ships, but with this city.
level.cahokia.source: Timothy Pauketat, "Cahokia: Ancient America's Great City on the Mississippi" (2009); UNESCO, "Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site"
level.haudenosaunee.title: The Great Law of Peace
level.haudenosaunee.goal: The Peacemaker, a grieving father, and a clan mother win over the most fearsome chief, and five nations unite in a League
level.haudenosaunee.hint: You can't comb out snakes by force. Heal the grief first, then win the word of the women, and only then go to Tadodaho.
level.haudenosaunee.intro: The forests of what is now New York State, around the 1400s. Five nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca, are drowning in blood feuds. The Onondaga are ruled by Tadodaho, in whose hair, legend says, snakes writhe. Hiawatha has lost his daughters, and grief has driven him mad.
level.haudenosaunee.fact: Haudenosaunee oral tradition tells how Deganawida, the Peacemaker, met the grieving Hiawatha and wiped away his tears with strings of wampum shell. That was the first Condolence Ceremony, which still opens councils today. The first to accept the Great Law of Peace was the clan mother Jigonsaseh; ever since, the League's chiefs have been chosen and removed by the senior women of the clans. Tadodaho was the last to yield: Hiawatha and Deganawida "combed the snakes from his hair," and he became the keeper of the council fire. The five nations buried their weapons beneath the Great Tree of Peace, a white pine. No one knows exactly when the League was founded; estimates range from the 1100s to the 1500s. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy still exists, and the Hiawatha wampum belt is its flag.
level.haudenosaunee.source: Haudenosaunee oral tradition (Gayanashagowa); Arthur C. Parker, "The Constitution of the Five Nations" (1916)
level.columbus_1492.title: Contact
level.columbus_1492.goal: Columbus seeks a route to Asia and finds the islands of the Caribbean instead, an encounter that will change both halves of the world forever
level.columbus_1492.hint: Spotting land is a sailor's job, and you can't build a fort without help from the island's hosts. Looking for the Great Khan is pointless: he isn't here.
level.columbus_1492.intro: October 12, 1492. Three Spanish ships have been sailing west for more than a month: the Genoese captain Christopher Columbus is sure it's the shortest way to China and the Indies. The queen has promised 10,000 maravedís to whoever sights land first. On board is an interpreter, Luis de Torres, a converted Jew who speaks Arabic; Columbus plans to use him to talk with the Great Khan.
level.columbus_1492.fact: The first to see land was the sailor Rodrigo de Triana, but Columbus awarded the lifetime pension to himself, claiming he had seen a light the evening before. On the island of Hispaniola, the Taíno cacique Guacanagarí welcomed the newcomers; when the Santa María ran aground on a reef on Christmas night, his people helped save the cargo, and the wreck's timbers went into Fort La Navidad, the first European settlement in the Americas. Columbus died still convinced he had been to Asia. He never set foot in what is now the United States, but 1492 began the "Columbian Exchange": horses, wheat, and smallpox came to the Americas, while potatoes, corn, and tobacco went to Europe. For Native peoples it brought enslavement and epidemics that killed most of the islands' inhabitants within a few decades.
level.columbus_1492.source: Diary of Columbus's first voyage (as abstracted by Bartolomé de las Casas); Alfred W. Crosby, "The Columbian Exchange" (1972)
level.st_augustine_1565.title: St. Augustine
level.st_augustine_1565.goal: A Spanish admiral founds the oldest city in the United States and wipes out his French rivals after a hurricane does them in
level.st_augustine_1565.hint: The city comes before the war. Attacking a strong fleet head-on is suicide: wait for nature to do its work.
level.st_augustine_1565.intro: 1565. Two empires and two faiths are fighting over Florida: French Protestant Huguenots have built Fort Caroline, and the king of Spain sends Admiral Pedro Menéndez de Avilés to drive out the "heretics." The land around them belongs to the Timucua, whose chief, Saturiwa, is a friend of the French.
level.st_augustine_1565.fact: On September 8, 1565, the chaplain López de Mendoza said Mass, and Menéndez founded St. Augustine, the oldest continuously inhabited European city in the continental United States. The Frenchman Jean Ribault led his fleet against the Spanish, but a hurricane smashed his ships on the shore. Meanwhile Menéndez captured Fort Caroline, then met the shipwrecked French at an inlet: they surrendered, and hundreds of them, Ribault included, were executed as Protestants. The inlet is still called Matanzas, "slaughter." Spanish Florida lasted more than two hundred years, and runaways from the English colonies would later flee here to the Spanish.
level.st_augustine_1565.source: Francisco López de Mendoza Grajales, "Memoir" (1565); Gonzalo Solís de Merás, "Memorial" (1567)
level.roanoke_1587.title: The Lost Colony
level.roanoke_1587.goal: The governor sails off for supplies, and when he returns three years later he finds only the word CROATOAN carved on a post
level.roanoke_1587.hint: The governor has to sail away, or there will be no return. The cross was the agreed sign of danger, and no cross was found.
level.roanoke_1587.intro: 1587. On Roanoke Island, off the coast of what is now North Carolina, about 115 English colonists land under the artist John White. His daughter Eleanor Dare gives birth to Virginia, the first English child born in America. With them is Manteo, a Croatoan man who has been to London and become a go-between.
level.roanoke_1587.fact: White sailed to England for supplies after agreeing on a signal: if the colonists moved, they would carve the name of their new location; if they were in trouble, a Maltese cross. For three years he couldn't get back, as England was fighting the Spanish Armada. In August 1590 he found empty houses and the word CROATOAN carved on a post, with no cross. A storm kept him from reaching Croatoan Island, and White never saw his daughter or granddaughter again. The colony's fate is the great mystery of early America: most likely the colonists scattered and merged with neighboring Algonquian peoples. Archaeologists are still finding English objects on Hatteras Island.
level.roanoke_1587.source: John White, account of the 1590 voyage (in Richard Hakluyt's "Principal Navigations"); David Beers Quinn, "Set Fair for Roanoke" (1985)
level.jamestown_1607.title: Jamestown and Powhatan
level.jamestown_1607.goal: A starving English colony survives thanks to Powhatan corn, tobacco, and Pocahontas's marriage to John Rolfe
level.jamestown_1607.hint: You don't make war on the people who feed you. A marriage seals the peace, but first the groom needs a way to make a living.
level.jamestown_1607.intro: 1607. One hundred and four Englishmen found Jamestown on a swampy riverbank in Virginia. All around lie the lands of the Powhatan Confederacy: more than thirty peoples under the paramount chief Wahunsenacah, whom the English call Powhatan. Only the corn trade keeps the colonists from starving.
level.jamestown_1607.fact: Captain John Smith bartered for food with Powhatan's people; he later claimed that the chief's daughter Matoaka, nicknamed Pocahontas, saved him from execution, but historians doubt that pretty scene. In the "Starving Time" of 1609–1610, colonists were driven to cannibalism. Tobacco saved the colony: John Rolfe brought in a sweet strain, and Virginia began to grow rich. In 1613 the English took Matoaka hostage; in captivity she was baptized as Rebecca, and in 1614 she married Rolfe, ushering in the "Peace of Pocahontas." In 1617 she died in England, where she had been shown off as a model of the "civilized Indian." In 1622, four years after Powhatan's death, war broke out again.
level.jamestown_1607.source: John Smith, "The Generall Historie of Virginia" (1624); Camilla Townsend, "Pocahontas and the Powhatan Dilemma" (2004)
level.virginia_1619.title: 1619: The Assembly and the White Lion
level.virginia_1619.goal: Virginia gets America's first elected assembly, and that same year the first documented Africans are brought to its shores
level.virginia_1619.hint: The assembly starts with a right granted by charter, and with elections. Heat and fever drive the delegates away, but the session must be seen through.
level.virginia_1619.intro: 1619. The Virginia Company wants to attract colonists and grants them a charter: the colony will make some of its own laws. Governor George Yeardley calls elections, and the colony's secretary, John Pory, will serve as speaker of the first assembly.
level.virginia_1619.fact: On July 30, 1619, the General Assembly met in the Jamestown church: twenty-two burgesses from eleven settlements. It was the first elected legislature in English America; the session broke up after six days because of the heat and malaria. In late August of that same year, the English privateer White Lion arrived at Point Comfort carrying "20 and odd Negroes," people from Angola seized from a Portuguese slave ship. They were traded for provisions. They are the first documented Africans in English Virginia; one of them, Angela, appears in the census of 1625. Their legal status was unclear at first, but over the following decades Virginia's laws made slavery lifelong, hereditary, and based on race. Freedom and slavery in America were born in the same year.
level.virginia_1619.source: John Pory, "A Reporte of the Manner of Proceeding in the General Assembly" (1619); John Rolfe, letter to Sir Edwin Sandys (January 1620)
level.mayflower_1620.title: The Mayflower Compact
level.mayflower_1620.goal: A storm carries the Pilgrims beyond the reach of their charter, and to keep from scattering, they sign their own agreement on how to govern
level.mayflower_1620.hint: No crisis, no need for a compact. Win over the man who wants to leave; don't just let him go.
level.mayflower_1620.intro: November 1620. After 66 days at sea, the Mayflower and its 102 passengers approach America. About forty of them are "Saints," Puritan Separatists who fled the Church of England; the rest are "Strangers," hired craftsmen and servants. They hold a patent to settle in Virginia, but a storm drives the ship far to the north.
level.mayflower_1620.fact: Outside Virginia the patent had no force, and some of the Strangers declared that once ashore they would do as they pleased. Among them was probably Stephen Hopkins, who in 1609 had already joined a mutiny of castaways on Bermuda. On November 11, forty-one men signed the Mayflower Compact in the ship's cabin, agreeing to "combine ourselves together into a civil body politic" and to obey laws made for the general good. John Carver was elected governor. A scouting party under Myles Standish found a harbor with fields already cleared by the Wampanoag, whose village had recently been emptied by an epidemic. Half the colonists died that first winter. No women signed the compact, but it became one of the founding documents of American self-government.
level.mayflower_1620.source: William Bradford, "Of Plymouth Plantation" (1630–1651); text of the Mayflower Compact (1620)
level.plymouth_1621.title: The Harvest Feast
level.plymouth_1621.goal: Squanto teaches the Pilgrims to plant corn, Massasoit makes an alliance, and in the fall of 1621 they celebrate the harvest together
level.plymouth_1621.hint: No harvest, nothing to celebrate, and without an interpreter two peoples can't reach an agreement.
level.plymouth_1621.intro: Spring 1621. Half of Plymouth's colonists have died over the winter. An Indian named Samoset walks into the settlement and greets them in English, and soon he brings Tisquantum, or Squanto, of the Patuxet people. Years earlier the English kidnapped Squanto and sold him into slavery in Spain; he escaped, lived in London, and came home to find his village wiped out by an epidemic.
level.plymouth_1621.fact: Squanto taught the Pilgrims to plant corn with a fish in each hill as fertilizer, and he interpreted at their talks with Ousamequin, the great sachem of the Wampanoag, whom the English called Massasoit. The alliance served both sides: the Wampanoag, weakened by disease, wanted protection from their Narragansett neighbors. That fall the colonists held a harvest celebration; Massasoit arrived with ninety men and brought five deer, and the feast lasted three days. No one called it "Thanksgiving"; it became a national holiday only in 1863, under Lincoln. Massasoit's alliance with Plymouth held for fifty years, until the war waged by his son Metacom.
level.plymouth_1621.source: Edward Winslow, letter in "Mourt's Relation" (1622); William Bradford, "Of Plymouth Plantation"

level.rhode_island_1636.title: Liberty of Conscience
level.rhode_island_1636.goal: A preacher banished from Massachusetts receives land from the Narragansett and founds the first colony where no one is persecuted for their faith
level.rhode_island_1636.hint: Repenting is easier than wintering in the woods, but then there will be no Rhode Island. Here the land is given by its owners, not by the king.
level.rhode_island_1636.intro: 1635, the Massachusetts Bay Colony. The Puritans fled England for the freedom of their own faith, but in their "city upon a hill" they tolerate no other. The preacher Roger Williams teaches dangerous ideas: the government must not punish people for their beliefs, and colonists must buy land from the Indians rather than take it under a royal charter.
level.rhode_island_1636.fact: The Massachusetts General Court banished Williams; warned by former governor John Winthrop that he was about to be shipped back to England, he fled through the winter woods in 1636 to the Narragansett, whose language he had learned. The sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi gave him land at the head of the bay, and he named the settlement Providence. Williams was the first in America to build a "wall of separation" between church and state; Baptists, Quakers, and Jews found refuge there. In 1638 Rhode Island also sheltered Anne Hutchinson, banished for being a woman who interpreted Scripture to men. Rhode Island's charter of 1663 guaranteed freedom of worship, more than a century before the Bill of Rights.
level.rhode_island_1636.source: Roger Williams, "The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution, for Cause of Conscience" (1644); Rhode Island Royal Charter (1663)
level.metacom_1675.title: Metacom's War
level.metacom_1675.goal: Massasoit's son rouses the peoples of New England against the colonists in the bloodiest war of colonial America
level.metacom_1675.hint: The war begins not with a raid but with a trial. One chief isn't enough: he needs allies. And the end of the war came out of the swamps.
level.metacom_1675.intro: 1675. Half a century ago, the sachem Massasoit made an alliance with Plymouth. Now the Wampanoag sachem is his son Metacom, whom the English call "King Philip." The colonies keep growing, Wampanoag land keeps shrinking, and English courts try Indians under English law.
level.metacom_1675.fact: In the summer of 1675 a Plymouth court hanged three Wampanoag for the murder of John Sassamon, a Christian Indian, and the war began. Metacom was joined by Weetamoo, sachem of the Pocasset, by the Nipmuc, and later by the Narragansett. Dozens of English towns were burned, and the colonies answered by destroying villages and selling captives into slavery in the Caribbean. In August 1676 Captain Benjamin Church's company, colonists fighting alongside allied Sakonnet Indians, tracked Metacom down at Mount Hope, where he was shot by an Indian named Alderman. Metacom's head was displayed on a pole in Plymouth for twenty years; Weetamoo drowned while fleeing. Per capita, it remains one of the bloodiest wars in American history, and it effectively ended the independence of the Native peoples of southern New England.
level.metacom_1675.source: Benjamin Church, "Entertaining Passages Relating to Philip's War" (1716); Jill Lepore, "The Name of War" (1998)
level.bacon_1676.title: Bacon's Rebellion
level.bacon_1676.goal: Virginia's poor settlers demand war on the Indians, burn Jamestown, and frighten the elite so badly that it bets on slavery
level.bacon_1676.hint: The rebellion starts with a strike against the neighbors, not the governor. Giving the rebel a commission means handing him the colony.
level.bacon_1676.intro: 1676, Virginia. Former indentured servants who have served out their years get their freedom but no land: the best of it has been snapped up by the rich, and to the west lies Indian country. A young planter, Nathaniel Bacon, demands that Governor William Berkeley make war on all Indians without distinction. Berkeley refuses: the Indian trade is profitable for him and his friends.
level.bacon_1676.fact: Bacon led a militia of poor white settlers, servants, and even enslaved Black men against the Indians, and he attacked the Pamunkey, longtime allies of the colony ruled by their queen, Cockacoeske. Then he declared the governor a traitor, drove him out, and on September 19, 1676, burned Jamestown. In October Bacon died of dysentery, the rebellion fell apart, and Berkeley hanged 23 rebels. In 1677 Cockacoeske signed the Treaty of Middle Plantation, which recognized her people as subjects of the Crown with rights to their lands. And Virginia's elite learned a lesson: an alliance of poor whites and Blacks was dangerous. In the decades that followed, planters replaced white servants with enslaved Africans and passed laws dividing them by skin color.
level.bacon_1676.source: Report of the Royal Commissioners on the rebellion in Virginia (1677); Edmund S. Morgan, "American Slavery, American Freedom" (1975)
level.pueblo_1680.title: The Pueblo Revolt
level.pueblo_1680.goal: Knotted cords count down the days to the uprising, and the Pueblo peoples drive the Spanish out of New Mexico for twelve years
level.pueblo_1680.hint: The revolt depends on the secret count of days. The governor will leave on his own, but only once his city is under siege.
level.pueblo_1680.intro: 1680, New Mexico. For eighty years the Spanish have ruled the Pueblo lands: missionaries ban the ancient ceremonies and burn kachina masks, settlers force people to work for them, and drought and Apache raids bring famine. Popé, a healer from San Juan who was flogged for "sorcery," is planning the impossible: an uprising of every pueblo at once.
level.pueblo_1680.fact: Popé sent runners out with cords of yucca fiber: each morning one knot was untied, and on the day of the last knot everyone was to rise. The Spanish captured two runners, and the revolt had to start a day early, on August 10, 1680. Pueblos that spoke different languages rose almost simultaneously; about 400 Spaniards were killed, including 21 friars. Governor Antonio de Otermín withstood the siege of Santa Fe and led some two thousand survivors south to El Paso. The Spanish did not return until 1692. It was one of the most successful Native uprisings against Europeans, and a statue of Popé stands in the U.S. Capitol.
level.pueblo_1680.source: Antonio de Otermín, dispatches (1680–1682), in Charles W. Hackett, ed., "Revolt of the Pueblo Indians of New Mexico and Otermín's Attempted Reconquest"; David Roberts, "The Pueblo Revolt" (2004)
level.salem_1692.title: The Salem Witches
level.salem_1692.goal: Two girls' fits turn into a witch hunt: those who confess survive, and the honest go to the gallows
level.salem_1692.hint: The terrible paradox of Salem: confession saved you, denial led to the gallows. The survivor is the one who tells the court what it wants to hear.
level.salem_1692.intro: Winter 1692, Salem Village, Massachusetts. The nine-year-old daughter of Reverend Samuel Parris and his eleven-year-old niece, Abigail Williams, are seized by fits. The doctor's diagnosis: witchcraft. Suspicion falls on the minister's servant Tituba, an Indian woman brought from Barbados.
level.salem_1692.fact: Under pressure, Tituba "confessed," described the Devil, and named other witches, and panic swept the whole county. The court accepted "spectral evidence": the girls claimed the specters of the accused were tormenting them. Those who confessed were not executed; those who refused to lie about themselves were hanged. The jury at first acquitted 71-year-old Rebecca Nurse, but her accusers fell into hysterics, the judges asked the jury to reconsider, and in July she was hanged. In all, 19 people were executed, and one more was pressed to death with stones. Tituba survived: she was sold to pay her jail fees. Five years later Judge Samuel Sewall publicly repented, and in 2001 Massachusetts formally exonerated all the convicted.
level.salem_1692.source: Records of the Salem witch trials (1692); Mary Beth Norton, "In the Devil's Snare" (2002)
level.zenger_1735.title: The Zenger Trial
level.zenger_1735.goal: A New York printer sits in jail for criticizing the governor, and the jury acquits him because what he printed was true
level.zenger_1735.hint: No newspaper, no case. To apologize is to fall silent; salvation lies with the jury, not the governor.
level.zenger_1735.intro: 1733, New York. Governor William Cosby has removed Chief Justice Lewis Morris for refusing to play along. Morris's supporters launch the New-York Weekly Journal, the first opposition newspaper in the colonies. Its printer is a poor German immigrant, John Peter Zenger.
level.zenger_1735.fact: The governor had copies of the paper burned, and in November 1734 Zenger was jailed for "seditious libel"; for ten months his wife, Anna, kept the paper going. Under the law of the day, truth was no defense: any criticism of the government counted as libel. Andrew Hamilton, a sixty-year-old Philadelphia lawyer, admitted that Zenger had printed everything but appealed straight to the jury: the truth is not libel, and the cause at stake was the liberty "both of exposing and opposing arbitrary power by speaking and writing truth." On August 4, 1735, the jury returned a verdict of "Not guilty." The law did not change after the trial, but the Zenger case became a symbol of freedom of the press, which half a century later would be written into the First Amendment.
level.zenger_1735.source: James Alexander, "A Brief Narrative of the Case and Tryal of John Peter Zenger" (1736)
level.stono_1739.title: Stono and Fort Mose
level.stono_1739.goal: Spanish Florida promises freedom to runaways, and the enslaved of South Carolina launch the largest uprising of the colonial era
level.stono_1739.hint: First, freedom has to become real: it needs an address. Then word of it has to reach the plantations.
level.stono_1739.intro: The 1730s. In South Carolina, enslaved Africans outnumber whites. Close by, two or three weeks' journey away, lies Spanish Florida, at war with the English, which has proclaimed that any runaway who becomes Catholic will be free. Francisco Menéndez, a Mandinka who escaped slavery, already commands a Black militia there.
level.stono_1739.fact: In 1738 Florida's governor, Manuel de Montiano, gave the runaways Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose, the first legally free Black settlement in what would become the United States, with Menéndez as its commander. On September 9, 1739, near the Stono River, about twenty enslaved men led by an Angolan named Jemmy, also called Cato, seized a store of weapons and marched south with drums beating and cries of "Liberty!", gathering others along the way. The planters' militia under Lieutenant Governor William Bull caught up with them that same day; about 25 whites and dozens of the rebels were killed. In response the colony passed the harsh Negro Act of 1740, which barred enslaved people from assembling, learning to read and write, or playing drums.
level.stono_1739.source: Dispatches of Lieutenant Governor William Bull (1739); Peter H. Wood, "Black Majority" (1974)
level.great_awakening.title: The Great Awakening
level.great_awakening.goal: An English preacher draws crowds of twenty thousand in the colonies, and even the skeptic Franklin hands over every last coin
level.great_awakening.hint: The more pulpits are closed, the wider the field: a sermon in a church draws only a handful. And the miracle happened to the biggest doubter of all.
level.great_awakening.intro: 1739–1740. A religious wave sweeps the colonies; it will be called the First Great Awakening. In Massachusetts, Jonathan Edwards preaches on the wrath of God. From England comes George Whitefield, a preacher whose voice carries for a mile. "Old Light" ministers such as Boston's Charles Chauncy consider it all dangerous hysteria.
level.great_awakening.fact: Many churches shut their doors to Whitefield, so he preached in open fields and in the streets, to crowds of up to 20,000 or 30,000. Benjamin Franklin, a deist and skeptic, worked out by ear that 30,000 people could hear Whitefield's voice, and he described a sermon in Philadelphia: he resolved to give nothing, then thought he would give his copper, then his silver, "and he finish'd so admirably, that I empty'd my Pocket wholly into the Collector's Dish, Gold and all." Franklin became Whitefield's friend and publisher. The Awakening split churches, gave rise to new Baptist and Methodist congregations, and taught colonists to argue with authority, a habit that would come in very handy thirty years later.
level.great_awakening.source: Benjamin Franklin, "The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin" (1771–1790); Jonathan Edwards, "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" (1741)
level.seven_years_1754.title: The Shot That Set the World on Fire
level.seven_years_1754.goal: A skirmish fought by 22-year-old Washington in the Pennsylvania woods sets off the first world war, and its outcome will turn the colonies against Britain
level.seven_years_1754.hint: One shot in the woods, and no one believes the French came in peace anymore. Surrendering and signing is part of the story too.
level.seven_years_1754.intro: 1754. The Ohio River valley: here the claims of French New France and the British colonies collide, and the land is home to the Shawnee, Delaware, and Mingo. Virginia sends 22-year-old Lieutenant Colonel George Washington. His ally is the Mingo leader Tanaghrisson, known as the Half King.
level.seven_years_1754.fact: On May 28, 1754, Washington's detachment and Tanaghrisson's warriors surrounded a French party in a wooded glen; the wounded commander, Ensign Jumonville, was reportedly finished off by the Half King himself. The French maintained that Jumonville was carrying a diplomatic message. A month later Washington, surrounded in the hastily built Fort Necessity, surrendered and signed a document in French that called Jumonville's death an "assassinat," a treacherous murder; Washington insisted he hadn't understood the word. So began the French and Indian War, and then the Seven Years' War, fought in Europe, India, and America. In 1763 France lost Canada. The British general Amherst stopped giving gifts to the former Indian allies, and the Ottawa leader Pontiac roused the peoples of the Great Lakes. To end the fighting, the king barred colonists from settling beyond the Appalachians, and the Proclamation Line of 1763 badly angered the colonists.
level.seven_years_1754.source: George Washington, journal of the 1754 expedition; Fred Anderson, "Crucible of War" (2000)
scene.angry_god_us: "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God"
level.stamp_act_1765.title: The Stamp Act
level.stamp_act_1765.goal: London taxes every sheet of paper in the colonies, and the colonists answer with a boycott, a mob, and the famous "No taxation without representation"
level.stamp_act_1765.hint: You can only repeal what has been imposed. Pay up and you admit London's right; to get it repealed, you need a voice inside Parliament itself.
level.stamp_act_1765.intro: 1765. Britain has won the Seven Years' War, but it has run up enormous debts and keeps an army in America. Prime Minister George Grenville decides the colonies should pay for their own defense. The Stamp Act requires stamps on newspapers, licenses, wills, and even playing cards.
level.stamp_act_1765.fact: The colonists did not object to taxes as such, but they were outraged that the taxes came from a Parliament in which they had not a single representative: "No taxation without representation." In Virginia, Patrick Henry pushed resolutions against the act through the House of Burgesses amid cries of "Treason!", answering, "If this be treason, make the most of it." In Boston the Sons of Liberty, led by Samuel Adams, hung an effigy of the stamp distributor Andrew Oliver from an elm, the future Liberty Tree, and wrecked his house; Oliver resigned. Merchants boycotted British goods. In the House of Commons, Benjamin Franklin answered questions for four hours and warned that stamps could not be imposed by force. In 1766 the act was repealed, but Parliament immediately declared its right to pass any law it pleased for the colonies.
level.stamp_act_1765.source: Examination of Benjamin Franklin before the House of Commons (1766); Virginia Stamp Act Resolves (1765)
level.boston_massacre_1770.title: The Boston Massacre
level.boston_massacre_1770.goal: Soldiers fire into a Boston crowd; one patriot turns it into propaganda, and another defends the soldiers in court
level.boston_massacre_1770.hint: Propaganda and the courtroom need the same spark. Justice demands that the accused have a lawyer, even if he's a patriot.
level.boston_massacre_1770.intro: March 1770. Boston, a town of 16,000 people, is home to some two thousand British soldiers. On the evening of March 5, a crowd surrounds the sentry outside the Custom House on King Street. Captain Thomas Preston brings a squad to his aid.
level.boston_massacre_1770.fact: The crowd hurled snowballs, ice, and clubs; someone shouted "Fire!" and the soldiers fired. Five people died. The first to fall was Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native descent, often called the first casualty of the American Revolution. Samuel Adams and his allies trumpeted the "massacre," and Paul Revere's engraving, showing soldiers firing on peaceful townspeople on command, spread through every colony. The patriot lawyer John Adams agreed to defend the soldiers at the risk of his reputation: "Facts are stubborn things." Preston and six soldiers were acquitted; two were convicted of manslaughter and branded on the thumb. Adams later called the defense one of the best things he ever did.
level.boston_massacre_1770.source: John Adams, argument for the defense (December 1770); Paul Revere, engraving "The Bloody Massacre Perpetrated in King Street" (1770)
level.boston_tea_1773.title: The Boston Tea Party
level.boston_tea_1773.goal: The governor won't let the tea ships leave, a town meeting gives the signal, and colonists disguised as Indians dump the tea into the harbor
level.boston_tea_1773.hint: The signal comes only when every lawful path is closed. Pay the duty, and the tea ends up in teacups, not the sea.
level.boston_tea_1773.intro: December 1773. Parliament has allowed the East India Company to sell tea directly to the colonies at a low price, but with a duty the colonists consider illegal. Three tea ships sit in Boston Harbor, one of them owned by the merchant Francis Rotch. Governor Thomas Hutchinson, whose sons are selling the tea, refuses to let them leave.
level.boston_tea_1773.fact: On December 16, some five thousand people packed the Old South Meeting House. Rotch went to the governor one last time and came back with a refusal. Samuel Adams then reportedly declared, "This meeting can do nothing more to save the country." It was the signal. About a hundred men, roughly disguised as Mohawk Indians, boarded the ships and in three hours dumped 342 chests of tea into the harbor, worth more than a million dollars in today's money. They touched nothing but the tea and even replaced a broken padlock. King George III answered with the "Intolerable Acts": the port of Boston was closed, and Massachusetts self-government was curtailed.
level.boston_tea_1773.source: George Hewes, participant's recollections, in "A Retrospect of the Boston Tea-Party" (1834); Benjamin L. Carp, "Defiance of the Patriots" (2010)
level.congress_1774.title: The First Continental Congress
level.congress_1774.goal: The colonies meet together for the first time: moderates propose reconciliation, radicals a boycott, and the king has already decided for them
level.congress_1774.hint: Reconciliation came within one vote of passing, but then there would be no boycott. The king needs something to respond to.
level.congress_1774.intro: September 1774. In response to the Intolerable Acts, twelve colonies, all but Georgia, send delegates to Philadelphia. For the first time the Virginian George Washington, the Bostonian John Adams, and the Pennsylvanian Joseph Galloway, who wants peace with London at any cost, sit in the same room.
level.congress_1774.fact: Galloway proposed a "Plan of Union": an American council presided over by a royal president-general, sharing power with Parliament. It was rejected by a single vote and later even struck from the record. Instead Congress adopted the Continental Association, a total boycott of British goods enforced by local committees. George III wrote to his prime minister that "blows must decide whether they are to be subject to this country or independent." Galloway became a Loyalist and left for England; Congress agreed to meet again in the spring of 1775, and by then the war had begun.
level.congress_1774.source: Journals of the Continental Congress (1774); George III, letter to Lord North (November 18, 1774)
level.lexington_1775.title: The Regulars Are Coming Out!
level.lexington_1775.goal: Two lanterns in a steeple, Paul Revere's midnight ride, and the first shots of the war at Lexington and Concord
level.lexington_1775.hint: First learn the route, then ride. The patrol on the road will catch the rider; what matters is that he gets there first.
level.lexington_1775.intro: April 1775. General Thomas Gage, governor of Massachusetts, secretly sends troops to seize the militia's arms depot at Concord and perhaps to arrest Samuel Adams and John Hancock, who are hiding in Lexington. But the patriots are watching the British every step of the way.
level.lexington_1775.fact: The silversmith Paul Revere had arranged a signal: one lantern in the steeple of Old North Church if the British came by land, two if by sea, across the Charles River. On the night of April 18–19, the sexton Robert Newman lit two lanterns. Revere crossed the river and rode for Lexington. He did not shout "The British are coming!", since the colonists still considered themselves British; his warning was "The Regulars are coming out." Adams and Hancock got away. On the road to Concord a patrol stopped Revere, and Dr. Samuel Prescott carried the alarm on. At dawn the first shots rang out at Lexington, and at Concord's North Bridge the militia put the British to flight, "the shot heard round the world," as Emerson would write. The ride became famous thanks to Longfellow's poem, published in 1861.
level.lexington_1775.source: Paul Revere, letter to Jeremy Belknap (1798); David Hackett Fischer, "Paul Revere's Ride" (1994)
level.bunker_hill_1775.title: Bunker Hill
level.bunker_hill_1775.goal: Militiamen fortify a hill above Boston overnight and let the British come within thirty paces: a defeat worth a victory
level.bunker_hill_1775.hint: Powder is scarce, so don't waste it at long range. The British will take the hill, but they'll pay a terrible price for it.
level.bunker_hill_1775.intro: June 1775. The British army is bottled up in Boston, surrounded by thousands of New England militiamen. On the night of June 16, Colonel William Prescott and his men secretly fortify Breed's Hill, next to Bunker Hill, where cannon could fire on the town and harbor.
level.bunker_hill_1775.fact: In the morning General William Howe led the redcoats in a frontal assault. The militia had little powder, and legend says they were ordered, "Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes!" Two attacks broke under point-blank volleys. The third succeeded: the powder ran out, and the militia fell back, fighting with musket butts. Dr. Joseph Warren, one of the leaders of Boston's patriots, was killed. The British lost more than a thousand killed and wounded, nearly half the attacking force. "A dear bought victory, another such would have ruined us," a British general wrote. Black militiamen fought in the battle too, among them Peter Salem, who by tradition shot the British major John Pitcairn.
level.bunker_hill_1775.source: General Gage's report (June 1775); Nathaniel Philbrick, "Bunker Hill: A City, a Siege, a Revolution" (2013)
level.declaration_1776.title: All Men Are Created Equal
level.declaration_1776.goal: Paine's pamphlet turns the colonies toward a break, Jefferson writes the Declaration, and Abigail Adams reminds them that liberty isn't only for men
level.declaration_1776.hint: A Declaration gets written when the public is ready for it, so the pamphlet comes first. Waiting on the king means missing the moment.
level.declaration_1776.intro: Early 1776. The war has been going on for nearly a year, but most colonists still consider themselves the king's subjects, fighting only his ministers. The moderate John Dickinson hopes for reconciliation. In January an anonymous pamphlet appears in Philadelphia, written by a recent English immigrant named Thomas Paine.
level.declaration_1776.fact: Common Sense argued in plain language that it was absurd for an island to rule a continent, and that the king was no father of his people but one of the "crowned ruffians." In a year about a hundred thousand copies circulated among two and a half million inhabitants. That spring Abigail Adams wrote to her husband in Congress: "Remember the Ladies... Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands." John laughed it off. The Declaration was entrusted to 33-year-old Thomas Jefferson: "We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal..." Congress cut a passage from the draft that blamed the king for the slave trade, even though Jefferson himself enslaved hundreds of people. On July 2 Congress voted for independence, and on July 4 it approved the text. Dickinson refused to sign and promptly joined the army.
level.declaration_1776.source: The Declaration of Independence (1776); letters of Abigail and John Adams (March–April 1776); Thomas Paine, "Common Sense" (1776)
level.trenton_1776.title: Crossing the Delaware
level.trenton_1776.goal: Washington's battered army crosses the Delaware in a Christmas blizzard and captures the Hessian garrison at Trenton
level.trenton_1776.hint: No boats, no attack. Surprise depends on the enemy's carelessness; above all, the warning must go unread.
level.trenton_1776.intro: December 1776. New York is lost, and Washington's army is beaten and melting away: many enlistments expire on the last day of the year, and men are marching barefoot through the snow. Across the Delaware, at Trenton, sit the Hessians, German troops hired by the British Crown, under Colonel Johann Rall.
level.trenton_1776.fact: On Christmas night, through a blizzard and drifting ice, the fishermen and sailors of John Glover's Marblehead regiment ferried 2,400 men and Henry Knox's cannon across the river. Legend has it that Rall, busy at cards, was handed a Loyalist's note warning of the Americans' approach and stuffed it in his pocket unread; it was found on him after the battle. The dawn attack on December 26 lasted less than an hour: nearly a thousand Hessians were captured, Rall was mortally wounded, and the Americans lost only a handful of men. A week later Washington won again at Princeton. Many soldiers stayed with the army, and the Revolution was saved. The famous painting "Washington Crossing the Delaware" was painted in 1851 by the German-American artist Emanuel Leutze.
level.trenton_1776.source: Washington's dispatches to Congress (December 1776); David Hackett Fischer, "Washington's Crossing" (2004)
level.saratoga_1777.title: Saratoga
level.saratoga_1777.goal: A Polish engineer fortifies the heights, Arnold charges without orders, and a British army surrenders as France enters the war
level.saratoga_1777.hint: The cautious general will win by sitting behind his works; someone else will do the attacking. Only a beaten army surrenders.
level.saratoga_1777.intro: 1777. General John Burgoyne, a society darling and playwright, leads an army south from Canada down the Hudson to cut New England off from the other colonies. He is met by the Americans under General Horatio Gates. In the American camp are the Polish military engineer Tadeusz Kościuszko and the ambitious General Benedict Arnold, who is feuding with Gates.
level.saratoga_1777.fact: Kościuszko chose and fortified Bemis Heights, blocking the road to Albany. On October 7, Arnold, whom Gates had relieved of command, rode into battle without orders and led the attack that decided the day; a bullet shattered the same leg that had been wounded at Quebec. On October 17 the surrounded Burgoyne surrendered nearly six thousand men at Saratoga. Gates got the laurels. The biggest consequence was diplomatic: on hearing of Saratoga, France signed an alliance with the United States in February 1778, and Spain and the Netherlands followed it into the war. Saratoga's battlefield park has a strange monument: a boot with no name on it, honoring the leg of Arnold, who would later be branded a traitor.
level.saratoga_1777.source: General Gates's report to Congress (October 1777); Richard M. Ketchum, "Saratoga: Turning Point of America's Revolutionary War" (1997)
level.articles_1777.title: A Country Without Money
level.articles_1777.goal: The Articles of Confederation create a union of states with no power to tax, and the army is saved by one financier's personal credit
level.articles_1777.hint: The printing press won't help: the money is already worthless. You can only pay on the strength of someone's good name.
level.articles_1777.intro: 1777. The Articles of Confederation, the first constitution of the United States, are being drafted. Their author, John Dickinson, and most of the delegates fear a strong government: they have only just gotten rid of a king. So the union becomes a "league of friendship" among thirteen nearly independent states. Congress can declare war but cannot levy taxes; it can only ask the states for money.
level.articles_1777.fact: The Articles did not take effect until 1781. The states paid Congress little and grudgingly, so Congress printed paper "Continental dollars"; by 1780 they were so worthless that people said a thing was "not worth a Continental." Soldiers went months without pay, and some mutinied. In 1781 the Superintendent of Finance, Robert Morris, began issuing notes on his own name, "Morris notes," and founded the Bank of North America; that is how the army got the money for the march to Yorktown. The weakness of the Articles would become the main argument for a new Constitution, and Morris himself, once the richest man in America, would spend three years in debtors' prison and die soon after his release.
level.articles_1777.source: The Articles of Confederation (1777–1781); Charles Rappleye, "Robert Morris: Financier of the American Revolution" (2010)
level.valley_forge_1778.title: Valley Forge
level.valley_forge_1778.goal: A starving winter in camp becomes the army's school: a Prussian baron teaches it to drill, and a Polish count gives it a cavalry
level.valley_forge_1778.hint: Send the army home and there will be no one left to train. The foreigners didn't come to fight in the Americans' place, but to teach them.
level.valley_forge_1778.intro: Winter 1777–1778. The British have taken the capital, Philadelphia. Washington's army, about 12,000 men, goes into winter quarters at Valley Forge, some twenty miles from the city. Food, clothing, and shoes are scarce; thousands fall ill. Foreign volunteers begin arriving in camp.
level.valley_forge_1778.fact: About two thousand men died in camp that winter, more from typhus, dysentery, and smallpox than from the cold. But the army that marched out in the spring was a different one. The Prussian officer Baron Friedrich von Steuben, who spoke almost no English, personally drilled a "model company," which then drilled the rest; his "Blue Book" drill manual served the U.S. Army for decades. The Polish count Casimir Pulaski, a hero of the Bar Confederation, created the first American cavalry and is called the "father of the American cavalry"; he was killed at Savannah in 1779. The 20-year-old French Marquis de Lafayette served without pay and became almost a son to Washington. In June 1778 the retrained army held its own against the British at Monmouth.
level.valley_forge_1778.source: Friedrich von Steuben, "Regulations for the Order and Discipline of the Troops of the United States" (1779); Wayne Bodle, "The Valley Forge Winter" (2002)
level.arnold_1780.title: Arnold's Treason
level.arnold_1780.goal: The hero of Saratoga sells the fortress of West Point to the British, and the plot unravels when militiamen find the plans in a British major's boot
level.arnold_1780.hint: Treason begins with letters. The major will be caught only if he travels in disguise, and then the general's only option is to flee.
level.arnold_1780.intro: 1780. Benedict Arnold is one of the Revolution's finest generals, the hero of Quebec and Saratoga. But he is passed over for honors, Congress court-martials him over his accounts, and his young wife, Peggy Shippen, from a Loyalist family, lives in luxury. Arnold lobbies for command of the key fortress of West Point on the Hudson.
level.arnold_1780.fact: Through Peggy, an old acquaintance of the British major John André, Arnold opened a correspondence with the British and agreed to surrender West Point for £20,000. After a secret meeting, André headed back through no-man's-land in civilian clothes, carrying a pass from Arnold. On September 23, 1780, near Tarrytown, three militiamen stopped him and found the fortress plans in his boot. When Arnold learned of the arrest over breakfast, he fled to the British sloop Vulture, just hours before Washington arrived. André was hanged as a spy; even the Americans pitied the charming major. Arnold became a British general and fought against his own countrymen, and in the United States his name still means "traitor."
level.arnold_1780.source: Proceedings of the board of general officers in the case of Major André (1780); Nathaniel Philbrick, "Valiant Ambition" (2016)
level.yorktown_1781.title: Yorktown
level.yorktown_1781.goal: Washington pretends to attack New York, slips off to Virginia with the French instead, and traps Cornwallis at Yorktown
level.yorktown_1781.hint: The main blow lands where no one expects it. Washington himself wanted to storm New York, but victory was waiting in the south.
level.yorktown_1781.intro: Summer 1781. The British general Charles Cornwallis and eight thousand troops make camp at Yorktown on Chesapeake Bay to await the fleet. Washington sits outside New York, dreaming of storming it. Nearby is the French corps of the Comte de Rochambeau, while in Virginia Lafayette holds Cornwallis in check with a small force.
level.yorktown_1781.fact: On learning that Admiral de Grasse's French fleet was sailing for the Chesapeake, Washington and Rochambeau gambled on a risky plan. Outside New York they built camps and bread ovens so the British commander, Clinton, would expect an assault, while the armies secretly marched south, some 400 miles. On September 5, de Grasse drove off the British fleet at the Virginia Capes and cut Yorktown off from the sea. After a three-week siege, on October 19, 1781, Cornwallis surrendered; claiming illness, he did not attend the ceremony. Legend says the British band played "The World Turned Upside Down." The major fighting was over, and in London Prime Minister North exclaimed, "Oh God! It is all over!"
level.yorktown_1781.source: George Washington, diary for 1781; Nathaniel Philbrick, "In the Hurricane's Eye" (2018)
level.paris_1783.title: The Treaty of Paris
level.paris_1783.goal: American diplomats defy their orders from Congress and cut a secret deal with Britain, and Franklin somehow keeps the United States from falling out with France
level.paris_1783.hint: Following instructions means waiting forever. But once the peace is signed, the offended ally will need soothing.
level.paris_1783.intro: 1782, Paris. Three Americans are negotiating peace with Britain: 76-year-old Benjamin Franklin, darling of the Paris salons; the blunt John Adams; and John Jay of New York. Congress has ordered them to do nothing without the consent of the French foreign minister, Vergennes. But Jay suspects that France and its ally Spain want to pen the United States in east of the Appalachians.
level.paris_1783.fact: Jay and Adams persuaded Franklin to negotiate secretly with the British behind France's back. A preliminary treaty was signed on November 30, 1782, and the Treaty of Paris on September 3, 1783: Britain recognized American independence and ceded the lands as far as the Mississippi. Vergennes was offended, since the allies had broken their word, but Franklin wrote him such a letter that the minister not only forgave them but granted a new loan. The treaty said nothing about the Native nations that had fought for Britain: the British simply "handed over" their lands to the United States. Nor did it settle the question of slavery; that was left to the new nation.
level.paris_1783.source: The Treaty of Paris (1783); Richard B. Morris, "The Peacemakers: The Great Powers and American Independence" (1965)
level.shays_1786.title: Shays' Rebellion
level.shays_1786.goal: Massachusetts veterans turned farmers rise up against their debts, and a frightened elite calls the convention that will write the Constitution
level.shays_1786.hint: Forgiven debts would have given no reason for a Constitution. Only a real rebellion could alarm a retired general.
level.shays_1786.intro: 1786. The war is won, but Massachusetts is in crisis. The state demands taxes in hard coin, which farmers don't have; courts seize farms for debt and throw debtors in jail. Many of the debtors are Revolutionary veterans who were never paid. A former Continental Army captain, Daniel Shays, finds himself at the head of the discontented.
level.shays_1786.fact: Armed farmers shut down courts so they could not order foreclosures. Governor James Bowdoin raised a militia paid for by Boston merchants. On January 25, 1787, Shays's men marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield and were scattered by grapeshot; General Benjamin Lincoln finished off the rebels in February. Shays fled and was later pardoned. The uprising alarmed the elite across the country: under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could not even raise an army. George Washington, retired to his estate, wrote that the country was "fast verging to anarchy and confusion," and agreed to go to the convention in Philadelphia. A debtors' revolt thus became one of the parents of the Constitution.
level.shays_1786.source: Letters of George Washington (November 1786 – March 1787); Leonard L. Richards, "Shays's Rebellion: The American Revolution's Final Battle" (2002)
level.constitution_1787.title: The Constitution
level.constitution_1787.goal: Behind closed doors in Philadelphia, delegates argue all summer, and out comes the Constitution, followed by the Bill of Rights
level.constitution_1787.hint: Compromise is possible as long as the arguments stay off the street. The rights get written down only when someone refuses to sign without them.
level.constitution_1787.intro: Summer 1787, Philadelphia. Fifty-five delegates gather to "fix" the Articles of Confederation and decide to write a new constitution instead. They meet behind closed doors and shut windows in the summer heat. Washington presides; the chief architect is young James Madison, who keeps meticulous notes.
level.constitution_1787.fact: The large states wanted representation by population; the small states wanted an equal vote. Roger Sherman of Connecticut proposed the Great Compromise: a House of Representatives apportioned by population and a Senate with two members from each state. Southerners won the right to count enslaved people as "three fifths" in tallying population, a formula for representation and taxes that gave slaveholding states extra seats in Congress. The word "slavery" never appears in the Constitution. On September 17, 39 delegates signed it; George Mason refused because it had no bill of rights. Hamilton, Madison, and Jay campaigned for ratification in the newspapers, in essays known as The Federalist Papers. In 1789 Madison introduced amendments in Congress, and in 1791 ten of them, the Bill of Rights, were ratified.
level.constitution_1787.source: James Madison, "Notes of Debates in the Federal Convention of 1787"; the U.S. Constitution and the Bill of Rights
