level.exclusion_1882.title: America's Doors
level.exclusion_1882.goal: For the first time the United States bars Chinese laborers from entering, and in those same years a poet writes "Give me your tired" for the Statue of Liberty
level.exclusion_1882.hint: The exclusion law has to exist first; only then is there something to sue over. Two faces of America in one level.
level.exclusion_1882.intro: The 1870s, California. Chinese workers built the railroads and labored in the mines and laundries. When hard times came, they were blamed for "stealing jobs." An Irish immigrant named Denis Kearney gathers crowds on San Francisco's sandlots under the slogan "The Chinese must go!"
level.exclusion_1882.fact: In 1882 President Chester Arthur signed the Chinese Exclusion Act, the first major federal law to shut out a group by national origin: Chinese laborers. It remained in force until 1943. But in 1898 the Supreme Court decided the case of Wong Kim Ark, the San Francisco-born son of Chinese immigrants: under the 14th Amendment, everyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen, and that cannot be taken away. This birthright citizenship still holds today. And in 1883 the New York poet Emma Lazarus wrote the sonnet "The New Colossus" for an auction to fund the Statue of Liberty's pedestal: "Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free." The statue was unveiled in 1886, and from 1892 about twelve million immigrants passed through nearby Ellis Island.
level.exclusion_1882.source: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882); United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898); Emma Lazarus, "The New Colossus" (1883)
level.bridge_current_1883.title: The Bridge and the Current
level.bridge_current_1883.goal: The wife of a bedridden engineer finishes the Brooklyn Bridge, while Edison and Tesla fight over which current will light America
level.bridge_current_1883.hint: If not for her husband's illness, Emily would never have taken charge of the work. To win the War of the Currents, you need a rival who has already turned on the lights.
level.bridge_current_1883.intro: The 1870s and 1880s. America is building. Over the East River rise the towers of the Brooklyn Bridge, the longest suspension bridge in the world. John Roebling designed it, and after his death his son Washington runs the work, laboring in caissons on the riverbed. In New Jersey, Thomas Edison is building an electric lighting system at his "invention factory" in Menlo Park.
level.bridge_current_1883.fact: Washington Roebling was stricken with caisson disease and could not leave the house; he watched the bridge through a telescope from his window. His wife, Emily, taught herself higher mathematics, cable calculations, and the strength of materials, and for eleven years she effectively ran the project, relaying instructions and negotiating with contractors. When the bridge opened on May 24, 1883, she was the first to ride across it. Edison did not invent the incandescent bulb as such, but he created a practical bulb and an entire system: in 1882 his Pearl Street Station brought light to Manhattan homes with direct current. The Serbian engineer Nikola Tesla, who had worked for Edison, championed alternating current, which could be sent over long distances. In the War of the Currents, Edison tried to scare the public about the dangers of AC, but Tesla and Westinghouse won: in 1893 they lit the World's Fair in Chicago, and in 1896 the Niagara Falls power plant went online.
level.bridge_current_1883.source: David McCullough, "The Great Bridge" (1972); Jill Jonnes, "Empires of Light" (2003)
level.haymarket_1886.title: Haymarket
level.haymarket_1886.goal: The fight for the eight-hour day, a bomb at a Chicago rally, and an unjust trial: this is why the world celebrates May Day
level.haymarket_1886.hint: The chain: strike, rally, trial. Gompers's union is a different path for the labor movement that same spring.
level.haymarket_1886.intro: 1886, Chicago. Workers toil 10 to 14 hours a day, six days a week. On May 1, hundreds of thousands of people across the country go on strike for the eight-hour day. Among the leaders in Chicago are anarchists: the American Albert Parsons; his wife, Lucy, born into slavery; and the German immigrant editor August Spies.
level.haymarket_1886.fact: On May 3, police shot strikers outside the McCormick works. The next evening a peaceful protest rally was held in Haymarket Square; as police moved to break it up, someone threw a bomb. Seven policemen were killed, along with several workers in the gunfire that followed. Who threw the bomb was never established. Eight anarchists were tried for incitement, though most of them had not even been in the square; four, including Parsons and Spies, were hanged in 1887. From the scaffold Spies cried out: "The time will come when our silence will be more powerful than the voices you strangle today." In 1893 the governor of Illinois pardoned the survivors, declaring the trial unjust. In memory of Haymarket, May 1 became Labor Day in almost every country in the world, except the United States itself. In December of that same year, the former cigar maker Samuel Gompers founded the American Federation of Labor, a moderate union federation that fought not for revolution but for wages and hours.
level.haymarket_1886.source: Governor John P. Altgeld, "Reasons for Pardoning Fielden, Neebe and Schwab" (1893); James Green, "Death in the Haymarket" (2006)
level.dawes_wounded_knee_1890.title: The Dawes Act and Wounded Knee
level.dawes_wounded_knee_1890.goal: A law carves Native lands into allotments, the Ghost Dance alarms the authorities, and at Wounded Knee Creek the army massacres hundreds of Lakota
level.dawes_wounded_knee_1890.hint: The land is taken by law, not only by guns. The tragedy at Wounded Knee was not a battle but a massacre.
level.dawes_wounded_knee_1890.intro: 1887. The wars on the Plains are over, the nations have been forced onto reservations, and the buffalo are nearly exterminated. A reform-minded senator, Henry Dawes, believes he can help the Indians by turning them into farmers who own their land: tribal lands are to be divided into family allotments of 160 acres. And in 1889–1890 a new faith spreads across the reservations, the Ghost Dance: dance, and the dead ancestors and the buffalo will return, and the whites will vanish.
level.dawes_wounded_knee_1890.fact: The Dawes Act of 1887 broke up tribal lands and sold the "surplus" to settlers; by 1934 Native nations had lost about two-thirds of their land. Children were taken to boarding schools where their own languages were forbidden. Kicking Bear spread the Ghost Dance among the Lakota, and the authorities feared an uprising. On December 15, 1890, Indian police came to arrest Sitting Bull, and he was killed in the struggle. The Miniconjou band of Chief Spotted Elk (Big Foot), who was ill with pneumonia, was on its way to surrender. On December 29, at Wounded Knee Creek, Colonel James Forsyth's 7th Cavalry began disarming the camp; a shot rang out, and the soldiers opened fire, including with rapid-fire Hotchkiss guns. An estimated 250 to 300 Lakota were killed, more than half of them women and children. Twenty soldiers received the Medal of Honor. It was a massacre, not a battle, and it is regarded as the end of the era of the Indian wars.
level.dawes_wounded_knee_1890.source: The Dawes Act (1887); Jeffrey Ostler, "The Plains Sioux and U.S. Colonialism from Lewis and Clark to Wounded Knee" (2004); Heather Cox Richardson, "Wounded Knee: Party Politics and the Road to an American Massacre" (2010)
level.workers_farmers_1892.title: Workers and Farmers
level.workers_farmers_1892.goal: Carnegie's steelworkers, Debs's railroad men, and the farmers of Kansas rise up against the Gilded Age of monopolies
level.workers_farmers_1892.hint: The owners break the unions, and the courts and the army take their side. The farmers choose not a strike but a party.
level.workers_farmers_1892.intro: The 1890s. The Gilded Age: Carnegie, Rockefeller, and Morgan amass unheard-of fortunes while workers and farmers fall further behind. Andrew Carnegie's steel is poured at Homestead, outside Pittsburgh. Western farmers are drowning in debt as railroads and banks dictate their prices.
level.workers_farmers_1892.fact: In 1892, while Carnegie was vacationing in Scotland, his manager Henry Clay Frick locked the workers out of the Homestead mill to break the union and hired 300 armed Pinkerton guards. The workers met their barges at the river: seven workers and three guards were killed. State troops broke the union. In 1894 Eugene V. Debs's American Railway Union backed the workers of the Pullman Company, whose pay had been cut while rents in the company town stayed the same, and trains stopped across the country. A federal court banned the strike, the president sent in the army, and Debs went to prison and came out a socialist. On the Great Plains, farmers banded together in alliances, and the Kansas orator Mary Elizabeth Lease was credited with urging them to "raise less corn and more hell." In 1892 the People's Party, the Populists, was born. In 1896 they backed the Democrat William Jennings Bryan, who thundered, "You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold!" He lost, but many Populist ideas later became law.
level.workers_farmers_1892.source: Paul Krause, "The Battle for Homestead, 1880–1892" (1992); Richard Hofstadter, "The Age of Reform" (1955)
level.plessy_1896.title: Plessy v. Ferguson
level.plessy_1896.goal: A New Orleans shoemaker deliberately sits in a "whites only" car to challenge segregation, and the Supreme Court makes it the law of the land
level.plessy_1896.hint: To challenge a law, you have to break it, openly and according to plan. The dissenting justice's voice will be heard half a century later.
level.plessy_1896.intro: 1890, Louisiana. With Reconstruction over, one Southern state after another passes segregation laws. Louisiana's law requires "equal but separate" railroad cars for whites and people of color. A group of New Orleans residents, the Citizens' Committee, decides to challenge the law and strikes a deal with a railroad that has no wish to pay for extra cars.
level.plessy_1896.fact: On June 7, 1892, the shoemaker Homer Plessy, one-eighth African by ancestry, bought a first-class ticket, sat down in the whites-only car, and told the conductor himself that he was "colored." He was arrested, exactly as planned. The case went to the Supreme Court; his lawyer, Albion Tourgée, argued that segregation branded people as inferior. In 1896 the Court ruled, seven to one, that separate but "equal" facilities did not violate the 14th Amendment. The lone dissenter, Justice John Marshall Harlan, a former slaveholder from Kentucky, wrote: "Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens." The decision gave legal cover to Jim Crow: separate schools, railroad cars, hospitals, and cemeteries, never equal in practice. It would not be overturned until 1954, when the justices would quote Harlan.
level.plessy_1896.source: Plessy v. Ferguson, 163 U.S. 537 (1896), with the dissent of Justice Harlan
level.empire_1898.title: The Imperial Turn
level.empire_1898.goal: The United States overthrows the queen of Hawaii, goes to war with Spain, and instead of the promised freedom wages war in the Philippines
level.empire_1898.hint: The annexation came in the middle of a war, after the overthrow. The Filipinos expected independence and got a new war.
level.empire_1898.intro: The 1890s. The frontier at home is closed, and the United States looks overseas: it needs markets, coaling stations for the navy, and bases. In Hawaii, American sugar planters control the economy, but the throne belongs to Queen Liliʻuokalani, who wants to return power to Native Hawaiians. In Cuba and the Philippines, rebels are fighting Spain.
level.empire_1898.fact: In 1893 the planters, backed by U.S. Marines, overthrew Liliʻuokalani; she yielded to avoid bloodshed. In 1898 the battleship Maine exploded in Havana harbor; the cause is still unknown, most likely a fire in a coal bunker, but the "yellow press" blamed Spain, and war began. Within a few months the United States crushed Spain and acquired Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines, while Cuba became formally independent under U.S. supervision. In the middle of the war Congress annexed Hawaii, even though most Native Hawaiians had signed a petition against it. The Filipinos, who had fought the Spanish under Emilio Aguinaldo, expected independence and instead got the Philippine–American War of 1899–1902, in which some two hundred thousand Filipinos died, most of them civilians. Mark Twain, a vice president of the Anti-Imperialist League, wrote that the flag should be redone "with the white stripes painted black and the stars replaced by the skull and cross-bones." In 1993 Congress formally apologized to Native Hawaiians.
level.empire_1898.source: Liliʻuokalani, "Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen" (1898); Mark Twain, "To the Person Sitting in Darkness" (1901)
level.teddy_1902.title: Teddy Roosevelt
level.teddy_1902.goal: The most energetic of presidents takes on Morgan and sleeps under the stars in Yosemite: trusts and nature on one agenda
level.teddy_1902.hint: The banker will offer to settle things quietly, and then the trust survives. Roosevelt discovered nature not in his office but by the campfire.
level.teddy_1902.intro: 1901. After President McKinley is assassinated, the presidency passes to his 42-year-old vice president, Theodore Roosevelt: former cowboy, hunter, and "Rough Rider" of the Spanish war. The banker J. P. Morgan has just created a giant railroad trust, Northern Securities. In the Sierra Nevada wanders the Scottish-born naturalist John Muir, demanding that the wilderness be saved from the ax.
level.teddy_1902.fact: In 1902 Roosevelt filed suit against Morgan's trust. Morgan came to the president and proposed: "If we have done anything wrong, send your man to my man and they can fix it up." Roosevelt refused, and in 1904 the Supreme Court dissolved the trust. Roosevelt didn't destroy every trust; he "punished the bad ones," and his program became known as the Square Deal. In 1903 he spent three nights by the campfire with Muir in Yosemite, once waking up under a blanket of snow, and said it was the best day of his life. As president he created five national parks, 18 national monuments, and about 150 national forests. His chief forester, Gifford Pinchot, believed forests should be used wisely; Muir believed they should be preserved untouched, and that argument among conservationists continues to this day. And the teddy bear is named after him, after a hunt on which he refused to shoot a bear tied to a tree.
level.teddy_1902.source: Theodore Roosevelt, "An Autobiography" (1913); Douglas Brinkley, "The Wilderness Warrior" (2009)
level.wright_1903.title: The Wright Brothers
level.wright_1903.goal: Two bicycle makers from Ohio build their own wind tunnel, and on December 17, 1903, a human being flies an airplane for the first time
level.wright_1903.hint: Someone else's tables are wrong, so test everything yourself. The airplane must not only rise but also answer the controls.
level.wright_1903.intro: 1899, Dayton, Ohio. Wilbur and Orville Wright run a bicycle shop. Their younger sister, Katharine, a teacher, is their rock and chief correspondent. The brothers read about the death of the German glider pilot Otto Lilienthal and decide that the central problem of flight is not the engine but control. The elderly engineer Octave Chanute helps them with advice.
level.wright_1903.fact: Watching birds, Wilbur came up with "wing warping," twisting the wingtips so the craft would turn. Their gliders on the sand dunes of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, flew worse than their calculations promised, and the brothers discovered that Lilienthal's tables were wrong. So they built a wind tunnel out of a box and tested some two hundred model wings. Their engine was built by the mechanic Charlie Taylor. On December 14, 1903, Wilbur won the coin toss, but his attempt failed; on December 17, Orville was at the controls: 12 seconds, 120 feet. They flew four times that day, the best flight lasting 59 seconds. The newspapers barely believed it. Five years later Wilbur dazzled France with his flights, and Katharine became one of the first American women to go up in an airplane.
level.wright_1903.source: The Wright brothers' telegram to their father (December 17, 1903); David McCullough, "The Wright Brothers" (2015)
level.panama_1903.title: The Panama Canal
level.panama_1903.goal: The United States helps Panama break away from Colombia, and ten years later opens a canal between two oceans
level.panama_1903.hint: The talks with Colombia have already failed, so the canal was won another way. The treaty is signed not by a Panamanian but by a Frenchman.
level.panama_1903.intro: 1903. Roosevelt wants a canal across the Isthmus of Panama so the navy can move quickly between oceans. The French have already tried to build one and gone bankrupt; their former engineer, Philippe Bunau-Varilla, is looking for a buyer for the rights. The isthmus belongs to Colombia, and the Colombian senate rejects a treaty with the United States.
level.panama_1903.fact: Bunau-Varilla and Panamanian separatists, among them the physician Manuel Amador Guerrero, prepared an uprising. On November 3, 1903, Panama declared independence, and the American cruiser Nashville kept Colombian troops from crossing the isthmus. Two weeks later Bunau-Varilla, whom Panama's provisional government had named its envoy, signed a treaty with Secretary of State John Hay: the United States received a canal zone ten miles wide "in perpetuity." The Panamanian delegation reached Washington after everything had already been signed. Construction took ten years; Dr. William Gorgas defeated yellow fever and malaria, but some 5,600 workers died, many of them from Barbados and Jamaica. The canal opened on August 15, 1914, in the same days that world war broke out in Europe. "I took the Isthmus," Roosevelt boasted. In 1921 the United States paid Colombia $25 million, and in 1999 it handed the canal over to Panama.
level.panama_1903.source: The Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty (1903); David McCullough, "The Path Between the Seas" (1977)
level.jungle_1906.title: The Jungle
level.jungle_1906.goal: A novel about the Chicago stockyards causes such a scandal that Congress passes the first food safety laws
level.jungle_1906.hint: Don't take the word of someone who inspects himself. The law will pass only when independent eyes confirm the scandal.
level.jungle_1906.intro: 1904. The young socialist Upton Sinclair spends seven weeks studying Chicago's meatpacking plants and talking with the workers, to write a novel about the lives of the immigrant laborers there. Meat barons like J. Ogden Armour insist their products are clean. In Washington the chemist Harvey Wiley has spent years testing food preservatives on volunteers, the "Poison Squad," and is demanding a food law.
level.jungle_1906.fact: The Jungle came out in 1906 and became a bestseller. Sinclair meant to expose the plight of Lithuanian workers, but readers were shaken by scenes of rats, rot, and even workers who had fallen into the vats ending up in the sausage. "I aimed at the public's heart, and by accident I hit it in the stomach," he said. Meat sales fell by half. Roosevelt, who disliked "muckrakers," the investigative journalists, nonetheless sent undercover inspectors to Chicago, and they confirmed much of the book. In June 1906 Congress passed the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act, the origins of today's Food and Drug Administration, the FDA. The condition of the workers the book was actually about hardly changed.
level.jungle_1906.source: Upton Sinclair, "The Jungle" (1906); the Neill–Reynolds Report on the Chicago stockyards (1906)
level.ford_1913.title: Ford's Assembly Line
level.ford_1913.goal: Henry Ford builds a car for everyone: the Model T, the moving assembly line, and five dollars a day
level.ford_1913.hint: First the car, then the line, then the wages. Raise the price, and the "car for everyone" becomes a rich man's toy again.
level.ford_1913.intro: 1908, Detroit. The automobile is a rich man's toy. Henry Ford, a farmer's son, wants to build a car his own workers can afford. His partner James Couzens minds the money, and the foreman Charles Sorensen hunts for ways to speed up assembly.
level.ford_1913.fact: The Model T came out in 1908, simple and sturdy. In 1913 the Highland Park plant launched the moving assembly line: the chassis was pulled past the workers, each of whom performed a single task, and assembling a car went from about 12 hours to an hour and a half. The work became unbearably monotonous, and workers quit by the hundreds. In January 1914 Ford announced the "five-dollar day," twice the usual wage, along with an eight-hour day. In return, a "Sociological Department" headed by the Reverend Samuel Marquis checked on how workers lived at home: whether they drank, whether their families were doing well. The price of the Model T fell from $850 to $260, and more than 15 million were built in all. "Fordism" transformed industry around the world, from Soviet factories to Japanese ones.
level.ford_1913.source: Henry Ford, "My Life and Work" (1922); David A. Hounshell, "From the American System to Mass Production, 1800–1932" (1984)
level.naacp_1909.title: The NAACP
level.naacp_1909.goal: The journalist Ida B. Wells exposes lynching, Du Bois demands full rights, and in 1909 the leading organization against racism is born
level.naacp_1909.hint: Booker T. Washington's compromise is the path of patience, and Du Bois chose another. The Association grows out of a movement, not a concession.
level.naacp_1909.intro: The 1890s and 1900s. Jim Crow laws rule the South, Black citizens have been stripped of the vote, and every week someone is lynched somewhere. The most influential Black leader, the educator Booker T. Washington, who was born into slavery, advises against demanding political rights for now: learn trades and build up property instead. W. E. B. Du Bois, who holds a Harvard doctorate in history, disagrees.
level.naacp_1909.fact: After friends of hers who ran a grocery store were lynched in 1892, the Memphis journalist Ida B. Wells began gathering data and proved that most victims were lynched not for crimes but because they were successful or "didn't know their place." Her press was burned, but she carried on in Chicago. In "The Souls of Black Folk" (1903), Du Bois rejected Washington's accommodation, and in 1905 at Niagara Falls he launched a movement for immediate equal rights. After the 1908 race riot in Springfield, Lincoln's hometown, the white reformer Mary White Ovington and others called on them to join forces. In 1909 the NAACP, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, was founded, with Du Bois as editor of its magazine, The Crisis. Forty-five years later it was the NAACP that would win the Supreme Court case striking down school segregation.
level.naacp_1909.source: Ida B. Wells, "Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases" (1892); W. E. B. Du Bois, "The Souls of Black Folk" (1903)
level.triangle_1911.title: The Triangle Fire
level.triangle_1911.goal: Seamstresses strike for safety, the owners lock the doors, and a fire that kills 146 people changes America's labor laws
level.triangle_1911.hint: This is a story of how it really happened: the price of locked doors. Perkins won new laws because she saw it all with her own eyes.
level.triangle_1911.intro: 1909, New York. Manhattan's garment shops are staffed mostly by young Jewish and Italian immigrant women working 60 to 70 hours a week. At the Triangle Waist Company, on the top floors of a tall building, the owners Max Blanck and Isaac Harris lock the doors so the workers can't sneak out scraps or take breaks.
level.triangle_1911.fact: In November 1909, at a mass meeting, 23-year-old seamstress Clara Lemlich cut off the union leaders' speeches: "I have listened to all the speakers, and I have no further patience for talk. I move that we go out in a general strike!" Some twenty thousand workers walked out in the "Uprising of the 20,000." Many shops gave in, but not Triangle. On March 25, 1911, fire broke out in the factory. One of the doors was locked, the fire escape collapsed, and the firemen's ladders reached only the sixth floor. A hundred and forty-six people died, most of them young women; many jumped from the windows as crowds watched. The owners were acquitted; later they paid the families $75 for each victim. Among the witnesses on the sidewalk was Frances Perkins. A state commission pushed through dozens of workplace safety laws, and Perkins became the first woman cabinet member in U.S. history, as secretary of labor, and she said the New Deal began on March 25, 1911.
level.triangle_1911.source: Report of the New York State Factory Investigating Commission (1912); David Von Drehle, "Triangle: The Fire That Changed America" (2003)
level.suffrage_1913.title: The Suffrage March
level.suffrage_1913.goal: Alice Paul leads women in a parade on the eve of Wilson's inauguration, Ida B. Wells refuses to march at the back, and the road to the 19th Amendment begins
level.suffrage_1913.hint: For Wells to take her place in line, she must not be sent to the back. The president will be won over not by the parade but by a silent picket.
level.suffrage_1913.intro: 1913. Women can vote in only a handful of Western states. A young Quaker, Alice Paul, trained by the radical British suffragettes, and her ally Lucy Burns are planning something unprecedented: a procession of thousands of women in Washington on March 3, the eve of President Woodrow Wilson's inauguration, when crowds will be pouring into the capital.
level.suffrage_1913.fact: About five thousand marchers paraded down Pennsylvania Avenue with bands and floats; a crowd of men attacked the procession while police stood by, hundreds of women were hurt, and newspapers across the country sided with the suffragists. The movement had its own racism: Black marchers were asked to walk at the back so as not to offend white Southern women. Ida B. Wells refused; during the march she stepped out of the crowd and took her place with her Illinois delegation. In 1917 Alice Paul's "Silent Sentinels" stood with banners outside the White House; they were arrested, and in prison Paul went on a hunger strike and was force-fed. In 1918 Wilson came out for the amendment, and in 1920 the 19th Amendment gave American women the vote, though many Black women in the South could not exercise it until after 1965.
level.suffrage_1913.source: Official Program of the Woman Suffrage Procession (March 3, 1913); Mary Walton, "A Woman's Crusade: Alice Paul and the Battle for the Ballot" (2010)
level.fed_reserve_1913.title: The Federal Reserve
level.fed_reserve_1913.goal: After a string of bank panics, Wilson creates the Federal Reserve System, a compromise between Wall Street and the Populists
level.fed_reserve_1913.hint: A bank handed entirely to the bankers won't get through Congress. The compromise: regional banks under government oversight.
level.fed_reserve_1913.intro: 1907. A bank panic: depositors storm the banks, and the system is rescued personally by the banker J. P. Morgan. It becomes clear that the United States, the only major country without a central bank, has no "lender of last resort." But Populists and farmers fear a central bank will become Wall Street's plaything.
level.fed_reserve_1913.fact: In 1910 a group of bankers led by the German immigrant Paul Warburg met in secret on Jekyll Island, Georgia, posing as duck hunters, and drafted a plan for a central bank. It couldn't be introduced openly: the Populists would have torn into a "bankers' bank." The new president, Woodrow Wilson, and Virginia congressman Carter Glass offered a compromise: twelve regional reserve banks overseen by a government board in Washington. In December 1913 Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act. That same year the 16th Amendment, on the income tax, and the 17th, on the direct election of senators, took effect. The lawyer Louis Brandeis, the "People's Lawyer," who wrote of the "curse of bigness" of monopolies, helped pass the Clayton Act in 1914 and create the Federal Trade Commission; in 1916 he became the first Jewish justice on the Supreme Court.
level.fed_reserve_1913.source: The Federal Reserve Act (1913); Roger Lowenstein, "America's Bank" (2015)
level.ww1_1917.title: The Fourteen Points
level.ww1_1917.goal: The United States enters the world war, two million soldiers sail for France, and Wilson offers the world a plan that includes an independent Poland
level.ww1_1917.hint: Neutrality ended with the telegram; there's no clinging to it any longer. Wilson's peace is born of war.
level.ww1_1917.intro: 1914–1917. Europe is at war, while the United States trades with both sides and stays neutral; in 1916 Wilson is reelected on the slogan "He kept us out of war." But German submarines are sinking ships, and in 1915, 128 Americans died aboard the liner Lusitania. The socialist Eugene Debs calls the war a slaughter for profit.
level.ww1_1917.fact: In January 1917 Germany declared unrestricted submarine warfare. The British intercepted and decoded a telegram from Foreign Secretary Zimmermann: Germany was proposing an alliance with Mexico and promising to return Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona to it. On April 6, 1917, Congress declared war. A draft was introduced; some two million men sailed with General John J. Pershing's American Expeditionary Forces ("Lafayette, we are here!"), and in 1918 they helped stop the last German offensive and break through the front in the Meuse-Argonne offensive. At home, the Espionage and Sedition Acts punished criticism of the war: Debs was sentenced to ten years for an antiwar speech. On January 8, 1918, Wilson set out his Fourteen Points, a plan for a just peace: open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, self-determination of peoples, and a League of Nations. The thirteenth point called for an independent Poland with access to the sea. On November 11, 1918, the war ended in an armistice.
level.ww1_1917.source: Woodrow Wilson, the Fourteen Points (January 8, 1918); the Zimmermann Telegram (1917); Michael Kazin, "War Against War" (2017)
